raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using a matched difference-in-differences design across Recife census tracts (1991, 2000, and 2010 censuses), municipal demarcation and land-tenure/urbanistic regularization of low-income settlements as Social Interest Special Zones (ZEIS) significantly increased household access to piped water and public sewage networks, while having null effects on the mean number of bathrooms per household and public garbage collection. Specifically, in dynamic DiD models separating medium-run (2000, 4-7 years) and long-run (2010, 14-17 years) exposure (Table 3), piped water network coverage showed no medium-run effect (+2.178 percentage points, SE 6.323) but a significant long-run increase of +15.702 percentage points (SE 7.105, p < 0.05), while public sewage network coverage increased by +15.471 percentage points in 2000 (SE 7.292, p < 0.05) and +23.479 percentage points in 2010 (SE 12.189, p < 0.10; and +18.970 percentage points, SE 9.187, p < 0.05 in pooled DiD with district trends, Table 2 Panel B).
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Pooled vs. dynamic horizon sensitivity for piped water: In pooled static DiD (Table 2), Water - public network is only significant at 10% without district trends (9.107*, SE 5.073, Panel A) and statistically null with district trends (8.086, SE 6.336, Panel B) because the medium-run 2000 effect is near zero (2.178, SE 6.323) whereas the long-run 2010 effect (14-17 years post-ZEIS) is +15.702** (SE 7.105, p < 0.05, Table 3). 2. Precision of 2010 sewage estimate: Although the authors emphasize the ~23 percentage point 2010 sewage gain in the abstract and text, in Table 3 Col (5), Table 4 Col (5), and Table 6 Col (5) the 2010 sewage coefficient is only significant at the 10% level (*, p < 0.10), whereas the 2000 sewage coefficient (**15.471, p < 0.05), the pooled Table 2 Panel B sewage coefficient (**18.970, p < 0.05), and the spillover-adjusted Table 5 2010 sewage coefficient (**28.612, p < 0.05) all reach p < 0.05. 3. Network utility vs. indoor dwelling sanitation: While public water and sewerage network connections improved, indoor Bathrooms/Households (dwelling physical structure) and public Garbage collection were consistently null across every table. 4. Minor Table 1 note wording slip: The note under Table 1 (p. 18) refers to utility variables as 'average percentage of homeowners accessing the service', whereas the main text (pp. 3, 5, 11, 17, 20-22) and figure captions (pp. 26-27) consistently define them as the percentage of households accessing the service; also Tables 1-6 label standard errors in regression notes as 'standardized deviation in parenthesis'. 5. Equations (1) and (2) on pp. 11-12 have missing embedded math symbols in the PDF text layer, though variable definitions in surrounding prose and all regression tables are completely intact.
raw_response.study_design: Quasi-experimental matched Difference-in-Differences (two-way fixed effects panel with Propensity Score Matching and district-specific linear time trends) across 3 decennial census waves (1991, 2000, 2010)
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Temporally compatible census tracts ('census tracks') in the City of Recife, Brazil (universe = 962 tracts across 1991, 2000, and 2010 censuses). Primary baseline pooled DiD sample (Table 2): 73 census tracts (19 treated tracts with >90% area under ZEIS implemented after 1991 + 54 PSM-matched non-ZEIS control tracts) x 3 waves = 219 observations. Primary dynamic DiD sample (Table 3, 1993-1996 cohort): 72 census tracts (18 treated + 54 PSM control) x 3 waves = 216 observations. Slum-control robustness sample (Table 4): 102 census tracts (18 treated + 84 non-ZEIS slum tracts) x 3 waves = 306 observations.
